transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-09
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO - Verdant AI), Marcus Wei (Platform Eng), Priya Sharma (ML Eng)

Summary: Quick discovery to understand Verdant's latency and throughput SLOs for their live document summarization endpoint; collect traffic shape and agree pilot scope.

--- Auto Sections (optional) ---
Topics: latency targets (p95), concurrency, streaming token/sec, hosted vs dedicated vs private, KV/prefix cache, security (SOC2, KMS), rollout plan
Action items: see metadata

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Thompson: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Ravi, our infra/SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Lena Ortiz: Doing good, Maya, thanks. We wanted to get into specifics on latency and throughput — we have a live summarization service used in the Verdant editor and p95 is a big deal for UX.
[00:18] Marcus Wei: Yeah hi, Marcus here. We're trying to decide whether to start on Hosted then move to Dedicated, or go Private from day one. Security bar is moderately high — SOC2 in flight.
[00:28] Ravi Patel: Great. Quick question — what p95 target are you aiming for for the human-interactive flows? 200ms? 500ms?
[00:35] Priya Sharma: For short summaries we want sub-700ms p95 if possible, ideally around 400-500ms for the 128-256 token outputs. But we also have longer reports where 1-1.2s is acceptable.
[00:45] Maya Thompson: That's helpful — so two buckets: low-latency interactive (<=500ms p95) for small outputs, and relaxed for long outputs. Curious what concurrency looks like — how many users in parallel?
[00:55] Lena Ortiz: Peak concurrency is about 120 active editors; average of 35 concurrent request streams, but bursts to 300 for certain releases. Typical session does streaming tokens — we stream partials to the UI.
[01:10] Ravi Patel: Streaming changes the equation — continuous batching & KV cache strategies can keep tail latency down. Do you cache prefixes or do you start each session cold?
[01:20] Marcus Wei: We don't have prefix caching currently. We do reuse some context within a session, but many sessions start cold with initial prompts.
[01:31] Priya Sharma: Also we've got multi-region customers. Latency from EU and US matters; we may require a regional footprint.
[01:40] Maya Thompson: Understood. For Hosted we can deploy regionally and use smart routing; Dedicated gives you control over capacity and predictable throughput. Private gives max control but more ops.
[01:52] Lena Ortiz: Can you break down token/sec and token-per-dollar so we can model cost for 300 concurrency bursts?
[01:58] Maya Thompson: Absolutely. High-level: token/sec depends on model and hardware. For example on a quantized Llama-3-ish open model, a single A100-class GPU at steady streaming might do X tokens/sec (we'll send precise numbers). For p95 we need to consider batching windows and cold KV misses.
[02:15] Ravi Patel: To give a real mapping — for interactive 128-token responses at sub-500ms p95, we often recommend Dedicated with reserved vcores if you have sustained or predictable burst patterns; Hosted may work if you accept variability or use caching + regional edges.
[02:29] Lena Ortiz: Is there a quick way for us to sanity-check? We can share a week of traffic shape and a sample prompt set.
[02:35] Maya Thompson: Yes please. If you share a token histogram and a small corpus of prompts, we can run a light micro-benchmark and give a recommended config. We'll include streaming and non-streaming results.
[02:44] Marcus Wei: On the security side, we need details on audit logs, KMS, and whether data at rest on Dedicated is encrypted with our keys.
[02:52] Ravi Patel: For Private/Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; audit logs are available in the Console. For Hosted, we provide encryption at rest and logs, but if you need key custody we recommend Dedicated or Private.
[03:07] Priya Sharma: Any pitfalls for streaming in Hosted — e.g., increased p95 due to batching?
[03:13] Maya Thompson: Streaming in Hosted uses continuous dispatch; we tune batching by latency SLOs. If latency SLO is tight, batching windows are small, which reduces throughput efficiency but keeps p95. With caching & prefix reuse, cost goes down and latency improves.
[03:27] Lena Ortiz: How do fallbacks work? If a model variant goes unavailable, can you route to a cheaper variant automatically?
[03:33] Ravi Patel: Yes, smart routing supports fallbacks to compatible model variants and regional failover. You can set policies: prefer low-latency up to a cost cap, then fallback to cheaper model.
[03:45] Marcus Wei: For our budgeting, can you put numbers: say 300 concurrent streams, average 200 tokens per response, 2.5 requests per minute per user during burst windows — how do we size Dedicated?
[03:57] Ravi Patel: We'll do a sizing run, but a rough calc: at 300 concurrent and 200 tokens per response, if you need sub-1s throughput per stream, you need aggregate token/sec of around 60k tokens/sec. Depending on model and quantization, that could map to ~4-6 A100-equivalent GPUs with optimized kernels and prefix caching cutting that by 25-40%. We'll formalize in the proposal.
[04:18] Priya Sharma: That estimate seems plausible. Do you support nvlink / multi-GPU model shards for lower latency?
[04:24] Ravi Patel: Yes, our runtime supports model parallelism and optimized kernel selection across NVLink clusters. For the lowest p95 we often colocate. For Dedicated we can provision NVLink-connected nodes.
[04:34] Maya Thompson: One thing we often run into — startup cold KV misses on first tokens cause p95 spikes. Caching strategy, warmers, or small reserved capacity can reduce those.
[04:42] Lena Ortiz: Ok, so immediate asks: a) sample benchmark harness, b) Dedicated sizing proposal, c) security deep-dive.
[04:48] Maya Thompson: Correct — we'll send those items.
[04:51]
[05:00] [timestamp jump, mid-call deep dive]
[05:00] Ravi Patel: Let's walk through a micro-benchmark plan: we run two passes — one synthetic token-generator that mirrors your token histogram, and one with your real prompts (streaming on). We'll measure p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and CPU/GPU utilization.
[05:15] Marcus Wei: How long does a run need to be to get stable p95? We worry about short-run noise.
[05:21] Ravi Patel: We recommend 10 minutes steady-state at target concurrency per region; if you have warm caches then shorter window is ok. For burst patterns we run 30-minute runs with ramp up and decay.
[05:34] Priya Sharma: For the real prompts, do we need to mask PII? We can't send real user content.
[05:40] Maya Thompson: Yes please mask or syntheticize. We can also run the harness inside your VPC for Private/Dedicated so data doesn't leave your environment.
[05:50] Lena Ortiz: Any internal telemetry we should surface? We use Datadog; can Redwood push metrics to our endpoint?
[05:56] Ravi Patel: We have exporters and OpenMetrics; pushing to Datadog is supported. We'll document which metrics are emitted (token rates, queue depth, batch size distribution, GPU latency histograms).
[06:10] Maya Thompson: On model selection: what model family are you planning? Open or closed?
[06:15] Priya Sharma: We're experimenting with Llama-style open models for cost, but we've got a small set of tasks that need higher quality — might need a closed model for those. Mixed fleet maybe.
[06:25] Ravi Patel: Mixed fleet use is common — route high-quality traffic to premium model, lower-quality to quantized open models. This is where smart routing and cost caps pay off.
[06:34] Lena Ortiz: For the Dedicated pilot, we'd probably start with a 3-month commit for cost predictability. What's the minimum sizing?
[06:40] Maya Thompson: Minimum reserved pool is typically 2 nodes (A100-class) — but for your burst profile we'd likely propose 4 nodes as a pilot. We'll include cost differences for various commit levels.
[06:50] Marcus Wei: Any differences in observability between Hosted and Dedicated? We want token-level traces and request->response mapping.
[06:57] Ravi Patel: Both have strong observability; Dedicated gives more retention and custom tracing hooks, and Private gives you the raw logs. Hosted includes token-level cost breakdown and per-model traces in Console.
[07:10] Priya Sharma: Are there limitations on streaming length or re-use of KV cache across sessions?
[07:16] Ravi Patel: KV cache is session-scoped by default, but you can configure longer-lived caches for predictable contexts. Streaming length isn't limited but you should plan for memory and kv-cache eviction for very long streams.
[07:28] Lena Ortiz: On SLOs: if we set p95 <=500ms, what are realistic SLA options?
[07:34] Maya Thompson: For Dedicated we can offer stronger latency SLOs in contract with penalties; Hosted has best-effort SLOs but high-perf profiles we publish. Private deployment allows you to set whatever contractual SLOs you need but depends on your ops.
[07:47] Marcus Wei: Do you instrument cold-start warmers? We saw a vendor use a 'pre-warm' ping which reduced tails.
[07:54] Ravi Patel: Yes, warmers are effective. We suggest scheduled lightweight requests during expected idle times or pre-warming before big releases. We'll include recommended warm-up cadence in the runbook.
[08:06] Maya Thompson: Quick note — pricing calculus example we'll send: tokens-per-second mapping to GPU-hours, and how caching reduces effective tokens.
[08:13] Priya Sharma: On quantization: if we go Q4 or Q8 we lose some quality — do you have evals to show tradeoffs?
[08:19] Ravi Patel: Yes, Redwood Optimize includes model/quantization recommendations tied to your eval prompts; we can run regression tests against your prompt set to quantify quality delta.
[08:31] Lena Ortiz: Perfect. Can we get a sample runbook for pilot? We need on-call rotations and escalation path.
[08:36] Maya Thompson: We'll include a pilot runbook and an on-call escalation matrix.
[08:40]
[12:10] [mid-call, later segment — timestamps not every minute now but every few minutes to reflect flow]
[12:10] Lena Ortiz: One question — if we pick Hosted to start, how quickly can we spin up regional capacity for EU?
[12:17] Maya Thompson: Typically within 24-48 hours for most regions, less for last-mile edge. We'll confirm region availability for EU and specific cloud providers.
[12:26] Marcus Wei: For the Dedicated sizing, what's the lead time for procured nodes?
[12:30] Ravi Patel: Depends on cloud/hardware; usually 1-3 weeks to spin up configured Dedicated pools. For on-prem Private it's longer — planning and airgap requirements add time.
[12:40] Priya Sharma: Regarding compliance — do you have SOC2 Type II, and can you share the report under NDA?
[12:46] Maya Thompson: Yes, Redwood has SOC2 Type II. We'll share the report under NDA and schedule the security deep-dive.
[12:52] Lena Ortiz: Great. Also need fine-grained RBAC for our product people.
[12:56] Ravi Patel: RBAC with role templates and SSO/SAML is supported; we'll show how to map roles to Console permissions.
[13:05] Maya Thompson: Anything else on performance side we should consider? Cold KV eviction, batch size limits, and affinity of requesters to nodes for locality — these affect p95.
[13:15] Marcus Wei: What about tail latencies at p99? It's important for SLAs.
[13:19] Ravi Patel: We measure p99 but p95 is commonly used for UX. For p99 we recommend additional headroom or dedicated, pinned capacity. We'll show p99 numbers in the benchmark.
[13:30] Priya Sharma: Can you support canary rollouts of model changes with A/B comparisons?
[13:34] Maya Thompson: Yes, the Console supports canary rollouts, traffic splits, and automatic fallback if quality or latency regresses.
[13:42] Lena Ortiz: Okay, let's lock next steps and timeline.
[13:45] Maya Thompson: Proposed timeline: share traffic + prompt samples by Wed 5/12 -> Redwood runs micro-benchmark and shares sizing + recommended config by Fri 5/14 -> security deep-dive week of 5/17 -> pilot decision week of 5/24. Does that work?
[13:58] Lena Ortiz: That works for us.
[14:01] Marcus Wei: One last tricky bit — during heavy burst windows we see queuing that spikes memory usage on clients; how do you recommend backpressure?
[14:08] Ravi Patel: Implementing client-side rate limiting + queue depth monitoring and using per-customer token quotas at the edge helps. Also set request timeouts and allow graceful degrade to summary-only responses.
[14:21] Priya Sharma: For pilot success criteria, let's define: p95 <=600ms for interactive, p99 <=1.8s, successful multi-region streaming, and cost target of X tokens/dollar that we'll refine.
[14:33] Maya Thompson: Good, we'll codify success criteria in the pilot doc.
[14:38] Lena Ortiz: Ok thanks, folks.
[14:41] Maya Thompson: Thanks — we'll follow up with the benchmark harness, Dedicated sizing options, and security scheduling.
[14:47] End of recording.
